meta.documentTitle: Mahabharat Episode 10: The Yadava Clan and Krishna’s Birth

header.title: Mahabharat Episode 10: The Yadava Clan and Krishna’s Birth
header.description: The origins of Yadu's lineage in Mathura, Kamsa's tyrannical rise, the miraculous rescues of Balarama and Krishna, and the interconnecting bonds between the Yadava and Kuru dynasties.

intro.title: Yadu's Council and Lineage
leads: While Puru's lineage led to the Kuru kingdom, his brother Yadu traveled south to the region of modern-day Mathura.

The local tribes in Mathura did not believe in kings or monarchy; instead, they were governed democratically by a central council. Cursed by his father Yayati never to sit on a throne, Yadu married into the Naga tribe and joined this governing council. Because Yadu eventually became chief of the council, all these unified tribes collectively became known as the Yadavas.

Generations later, Vasudeva was born into the clan alongside his sisters Preetha and Srutadevi. Their childless uncle, Kuntibhoja, adopted Preetha. Loving her deeply, Kuntibhoja bestowed his own name upon her, changing her name from Preetha to Kunti.

storyElements.html: Vasudeva wed two wives: Devaki and Rohini. Devaki had a brother named Kamsa, who was born out of a rape.

In most places, prevailing tradition dictating clan identity held that a child born to a mother belonging to a specific clan was accepted as a legitimate member. However, the Yadavas broke from this norm and rejected Kamsa, deeming him an illegitimate child. Despite his formidable skills as a warrior, they barred him from the governing council due to his vulgar and obnoxious demeanor.

Seeking power, Kamsa forged an alliance with King Jarasandha, a mighty ruler of the East. Backed by Jarasandha's massive military force, Kamsa rallied supporters, dissolved the ancient governing council, donned a crown, and proclaimed himself king—marking the first time in Yadava history that a monarch ruled over them.
As an undisputed, crude tyrant, Kamsa subjected his people to immense suffering. Shielded by Jarasandha's strength, no one could challenge him.
During his tyrannical reign, a prophecy cursed Kamsa that he would be killed by Devaki's eighth child.
Terrified, Kamsa immediately threw Devaki and Vasudeva into prison. As each infant was born, Kamsa personally grabbed the newborn by its legs and smashed its body against the stone floor.

storyElements.text: The Smuggling of Balarama and Krishna

storyElements.html: When Devaki conceived her seventh child, Vasudeva managed to secretly smuggle the baby out of the prison, swapping it with a stillborn infant found elsewhere.
The seventh child was carried safely across the Yamuna River to Gokula and placed in the care of Vasudeva's second wife, Rohini. This child was named Balarama.

When Devaki gave birth to her eighth child, occult practitioners were hired to cast a spell that put the prison guards into a deep sleep. Vasudeva carried the newborn boy across the Yamuna River to Gokula, where Nanda's wife, Yashoda, had just given birth to a baby girl.
Vasudeva swapped the infants—leaving the baby boy with Yashoda and bringing the infant girl back to the prison cell.

storyElements.text: The Unfading Prophecy and Infant Massacre

storyElements.html: The next morning, Kamsa stormed into the dungeon to execute the infant. Devaki desperately begged for her child's life:

bubble.text: It’s just a girl. It is not a boy who is going to grow up and kill you, this is a girl. She will get married and go away. Please spare her life.
Nothing doing, why take a chance?

storyElements.html: Kamsa snatched the baby, twirled her in the air, and hurled her toward the floor.
Instead of falling, the infant ascended into the air, transformed into a divine celestial form, and spoke:

bubble.text: The one who is to kill you is still around. I am not the one.

storyElements.html: Panic-stricken, Kamsa dispatched his army across the realm with strict orders to execute every infant under three months of age. While soldiers systematically slaughtered newborns throughout the region, the infant Krishna thrived safely in Gokula.
In summary, within the Yadu clan, Vasudeva had two wives:

* Devaki's only surviving child was Krishna.
* Rohini's children were Balarama and Subhadra.

* Srutadevi married Damagosha.
* Preetha (Kunti) married King Pandu of the Kuru clan, forging a vital link between the Yadavas and the Kurus.
